THE SEQUENCE AND THE RECOGNITION: A COMPARATIVE SYNTHESIS OF THE KRAMA SCHOOL AND THE IPVV

The Kālīs of cognition and the three powers — time, the akrama vimarśa, and the order-less support

  • magnum-opus essay. 2026-08-11. The Krama school of Kashmiri Śaivism — the "sequence" — makes time
  • d its goddess-energies (the Kālīs) central: consciousness is understood as a sequence of cognitive
  • ments, and the goddesses are the divinized powers of the cognition-process. The IPVV is the
  • cognition-philosophy's deepest commentary. This essay is the complete comparative synthesis of the
  • o. It shows that the Krama's sequence (krama) and the recognition's order-less (akrama) are two
  • ces of one claim: the order-less consciousness manifests as the ordered sequence, and the Kālīs of
  • gnition are the powers of the one consciousness. The comparison is grounded in the Krama material
  • ramasadbhāva, the Mahānayaprakāśa, the c1 studies) and the IPVV's L2 layer, and it is now possible in
  • ll because the IPVV is translated.*

PART I — THE TWO SCHOOLS

1.1 The Krama school

  • e Krama ("sequence," "succession") is one of the three great currents of nondual Kashmiri Śaivism,
  • side the Spanda and the recognition. Its central doctrine is that consciousness is understood through
  • s sequence — the ordered process of cognition, emanation, and withdrawal. And its central image is
  • e Kālīs — the goddess-energies who are the divinized powers of the cognition-process.
  • e Krama's key texts include:
  • The Kramasadbhāva ("The Arising of the Sequence") — a Krama scripture whose maṅgala (the project
  • s published the auditable translation of 1.8) invokes Mahākālī.
  • The Mahānayaprakāśa ("The Illumination of the Great Way") — Rājānaka Śitikaṇṭhācārya's
  • ilosophical synthesis of the Krama, with the daśākhaṇḍa (the ten divisions of cognition's
  • lumination) and the four-egg cosmology.
  • The twelve Kālīs (a Kālīkrama doctrine) — the divinized sense-organs and the powers of cognition.
  • e Krama's central insight is that time is not an obstacle but the very texture of consciousness.
  • e goddesses are not separate deities; they are the powers of the cognition-process — the sequence by
  • ich consciousness knows, remembers, and withdraws. As Wenta's analysis (in the Torella volume) shows,
  • he Twelve Kālīs constitute the analytical model of the cognitive process, with the sense-organs and
  • oughts accompanying sensory perception, pointing to the ultimate oneness of reality."

1.2 The recognition school

  • e recognition school (Pratyabhijñā) holds that liberation is recognition — the felt re-cognition of
  • e self as the Lord. Its deepest text is the IPVV, now fully translated.
  • e recognition school's central claim: the essence of consciousness is vimarśa, the felt
  • flexive-awareness — and recognition is the return by which the self re-cognizes itself as the Lord.
  • s account of time is precise: the order-less (akrama) consciousness manifests the ordered sequence,
  • d the "one who knows the order without being caught in it" is the order-less support (V2O).

1.3 The question of the comparison

  • e two schools are related — both belong to the nondual Trika, both come from Kashmir, and both were
  • conciled by Kṣemarāja. But they give different faces to consciousness and time:
  • The Krama: consciousness is the sequence — the ordered process of cognition, the Kālīs, the
  • śākhaṇḍa.
  • The recognition: consciousness is the order-less — the akrama vimarśa, the felt self-grasp that
  • nows the order without being caught in it."
  • The thesis of this essay.** The two are not opposed; they are two faces of one claim. The Krama's
  • equence* is the manifest face of the recognition's order-less; and the Kālīs of cognition are the
  • wers of the one consciousness. The order-less consciousness manifests as the ordered sequence — and
  • e Krama studies the sequence while the recognition studies the order-less that it manifests. The
  • quence and the recognition are one: the order-less is the source of the order, and the order is the
  • lf-articulation of the order-less.

PART II — THE CONVERGENCE: THE AKRAMA AND THE KRAMA

2.1 The shared claim: the source of time is not temporal

  • th schools agree on a claim that is striking in its precision: **the source of time is not itself
  • mporal.**
  • The Krama (and the TĀ's Krama passage).** The project's krama-time session drew out the Krama's
  • count of time from the TĀ's Krama passage:
"The sequence (krama) of emanation, persistence, and withdrawal are understood as three processes or
cycles (cakra) of a single process or cycle, which is the eternal activity of consciousness. **The
source of time, this activity is not definable in temporal terms as either a process, its absence,
both or neither.** Inexplicable in these, or any finite terms, the one reality is called the
Inexplicable." (the TĀ's Krama passage)
  • e tetralemma — "a process, its absence, both, or neither" — is the logical signature of a ground
  • ior to its own categories. Time is not illusory (not "absence"), not substantial (not "process"), not
  • mixture — it is the self-shaping of the non-temporal activity into succession.
  • The recognition (the IPVV).** The IPVV gives the same account, in the transcendental argument of the
  • der-less support (V2O):
"The pratibhā is the flashing — the light that runs through the ordered word-objects... It is
seasoned with their order, touched by it. But the flashing itself is not ordered. Its support — that
in which the flashing flashes, the one who knows the order without being caught in it — is the
order-less, infinite-consciousness-form knower."
  • The convergence.** Both hold that the source of time is not temporal. The Krama says the source is
  • ot definable in temporal terms as either a process, its absence, both or neither"; the IPVV says the
  • ashing is "seasoned with their order, touched by it, but is not the order." The order-less is the
  • urce of the order — in both schools.

2.2 The Present as the crack in time

  • th schools privilege the Present as the locus of practice — because it is the point where the
  • der-less ground is accessible.
  • The Krama (and the TĀ's Krama passage):**
"The practice is to cultivate a stable state (sthiti) of awareness of the Present in the centre
between the past moment that has ceased and the future moment that does not yet exist... The yogi
absorbs time into eternal consciousness even as he experiences how all things stream forth from the
immediacy of the Eternal Now and return to it."
  • e session's penetration: "the Present is the crack in time through which the non-temporal ground is
  • t." The past has ceased; the future does not yet exist; only the Present is the actual moment of
  • nsciousness, the pivot where eternity "descends" into time.
  • The recognition (the IPVV).** The IPVV gives the same point in the time-work: the un-brokenness of
  • e manifestation is what makes time-dealing possible (V2A). The "one who says 'I' across all of this"
  • lds the past, present, and future together — the one self who saw, remembers, and will see. The
  • esent is where the order-less self-grasp is met, because it is the point not yet absorbed into the
  • st or not-yet-real as the future.
  • The convergence.** The Present is the seat of the recognition: it is the crack in time through which
  • e akrama vimarśa is met. The Krama's practice (settle into the Present) and the recognition's return
  • e-cognize the self in the Present) are the same movement.

2.3 The Kālīs and the powers

  • e deepest convergence is structural: the Krama's Kālīs and the recognition's powers are the same
  • gnition-process, divinized or philosophized.
  • The Krama's Kālīs.** The twelve Kālīs (and the daśākhaṇḍa) are the divinized powers of the
  • gnition-process — the sense-organs, the thoughts, the moments of knowing. Wenta: "the Twelve Kālīs
  • nstitute the analytical model of the cognitive process." The goddesses are not separate deities; they
  • e the cognition-sequence made divine — each Kālī a moment or power of consciousness.
  • The recognition's powers.** The IPVV's powers (knowledge, memory, exclusion — jñāna, smṛti, apohana)
  • e the same cognition-process, philosophized: the powers of the one consciousness by which it knows,
  • members, and excludes. They unfold in a necessary order — manifestation → persistence → self-knowledge
  • self-expression.
  • The convergence.** The Kālīs and the powers are two maps of the same reality — the cognition-process
  • the one consciousness. The Krama divinizes it (the Kālīs as goddesses); the recognition philosophizes
  • (the powers as operations). Both are the self-articulation of consciousness into its moments and
  • wers. The Kālīs of cognition ARE the powers of the one consciousness, in the Krama's mythological
  • gister.

2.4 The daśākhaṇḍa and the sequence of the powers

  • e Mahānayaprakāśa's daśākhaṇḍa — the ten divisions of cognition's illumination — is the Krama's
  • ructured account of the cognition-process. And it corresponds to the IPVV's account of the powers'
  • folding.
  • e daśākhaṇḍa maps the moments of cognition: the arising, the persistence, the withdrawal, and the
  • ddess-energies that govern them. The IPVV's vimarśa-arc (from the pushing-ipvv session) maps the same
  • ocess: the powers unfold in a necessary order — manifestation (jñāna) → persistence (smṛti) →
  • lf-knowledge (apohana) → self-expression (kriyā) — and the whole converges on the one self-awareness.
  • The convergence.** The daśākhaṇḍa (the ten divisions) and the vimarśa-arc (the powers in order) are
  • o structures of the same cognition-process. The Krama sequences it into ten divisions; the IPVV
  • quences it into the powers. Both show consciousness as an ordered self-articulation, and both converge
  • the one that sequences it.

PART III — THE DIFFERENCES

  • e convergence is real, but the two schools differ in register and emphasis.

3.1 The register: mythological vs. philosophical

  • The Krama is mythological.** Its account of consciousness is expressed as goddesses — the Kālīs, the
  • śākhaṇḍa's divinities, the twelve. The cognition-process is divinized.
  • The recognition is philosophical.** Its account is expressed as powers and operations — knowledge,
  • mory, exclusion. The cognition-process is philosophized.
  • The difference is one of register, not substance.** The Krama's Kālīs and the recognition's powers
  • e the same reality, in two vocabularies. Wenta's point — the senses are "differentiated wonder"
  • iccamatkāra) — is the recognition's point that the powers are the self-awareness, expressed as
  • ddesses.

3.2 The soteriology: the sequence as the path vs. the recognition

  • The Krama's soteriology is the sequence.* The Krama path works *through the sequence — it does not
  • cape time but works with it. The yogin cultivates the Present, absorbs time into eternal
  • nsciousness, and so passes through the Kālīs. The sequence is the path.
  • The recognition's soteriology is the recognition.** The IPVV offers the recognition — the re-cognition
  • the self as the Lord, the "effort-less" means (V3P). The recognition cuts through the sequence rather
  • an working through it.
  • The difference.* The Krama works *through the sequence; the recognition works by the recognition
  • the order-less. But they are not opposed: the Krama's sequence is the manifest face of the order-less,
  • d the recognition of the order-less is the consummation of the Krama's path. The two soteriologies are
  • o phases: the Krama traverses the sequence; the recognition re-cognizes the order-less it manifests.

3.3 Time as divine vs. time as the mode of manifestation

  • The Krama divinizes time.** Time is not an obstacle but the goddess-energies — the Kālīs who are the
  • gnition-process. Time is sacred.
  • The recognition makes time the mode of manifestation.** The IPVV: time is the un-brokenness of the
  • nifestation (V2A), the appearance-order of the one light. The order is the mode by which the order-less
  • nifests.
  • The difference.** The Krama makes time divine (the Kālīs); the recognition makes time the mode of
  • nifestation (the order-less's self-articulation). But again, they are one: the divinized time (the
  • līs) IS the self-articulation of the order-less. The goddesses are the moments by which the order-less
  • nifests.

PART IV — THE COMPARATIVE TABLE

  • Theme | Krama | IPVV | Convergence |
  • ------|-------|------|-------------|
  • The source of time | not temporal (the tetralemma) | the order-less support (V2O) | the order-less is the source of the order |
  • The Present | the crack in time, the locus of practice | the seat of the recognition | the Present is where the akrama is met |
  • The powers | the Kālīs (divinized cognition) | the powers (jñāna-smṛti-apoha) | the same cognition-process, two registers |
  • The sequence | the daśākhaṇḍa (ten divisions) | the vimarśa-arc (powers in order) | the ordered self-articulation |
  • The soteriology | work through the sequence | the recognition of the order-less | the traversal consummated in the recognition |
  • Time | divine (the Kālīs) | the mode of manifestation | the divinized sequence = the self-articulation |

PART V — THE RECONCILIATION AND THE COMMITMENT

5.1 The reconciliation: two schools, one consciousness

  • e comparative synthesis yields a reconciliation. The Krama and the recognition are two schools of one
  • nsciousness:
  • The Krama studies the sequence — the ordered cognition-process, the Kālīs, the daśākhaṇḍa.
  • The recognition studies the order-less — the akrama vimarśa, the felt self-grasp that knows the
  • der without being caught in it.
  • The one claim: the order-less manifests as the order. The Krama studies the manifest sequence;
  • e recognition studies the order-less source.
  • e two schools are not rivals; they are two registers of the same nondual consciousness — the sequence
  • d its order-less source. And the IPVV itself acknowledges this: the transcendental argument (V2O) that
  • rives the order-less support from the ordered experience is the philosophical form of the Krama's
  • sight that the source of time is not temporal.

5.2 The historical lineage

  • e relationship is historical as well as doctrinal. The Krama and the recognition both belong to the
  • ika, and both were reconciled by Kṣemarāja (who wrote on the Spanda and the Pratyabhijñā). The
  • hānayaprakāśa explicitly links the Krama to the Śivadṛṣṭi and the Pratyabhijñā (from the project's
  • ssier: "the explicit yoking of the Krama-path to the Śivadṛṣṭi and the Pratyabhijñā"). The two schools
  • re not strangers; they were converging currents of the one nondual synthesis.
  • d the IPVV draws on the Krama material: the vimarśa-arc (manifestation → persistence → self-knowledge
  • self-expression) is the philosophical form of the Krama's sequence, and the sphurattā (the throbbing,
  • I) is the Krama's dynamic pulse. The recognition-philosophy is, in part, the Krama's sequence brought
  • the level of the order-less.

5.3 The shared commitment

  • d the two schools share the one commitment. Both assert the universal:
  • The Krama: the one cognition-process, the one consciousness through the sequence.
  • The recognition: the one Lord — all order-less supports are one (the universalization, A4).
  • th make this commitment, and neither forces it. The sequence of one consciousness and the sequence
  • another are asserted to be one sequence; the support of one field and the support of another are
  • mmitted to be one support. **The felt→ground step — from the per-field sequence/support to the
  • iversal — is the commitment both schools share.** This is the same wall the IPVV hits against the TĀ,
  • e Spanda, and every rival: the universalization is the Śaiva wager.

PART VI — THE SCHOLARLY CONCLUSION

  • e comparative synthesis of the Krama school and the IPVV yields five results:
  • The two schools are two faces of one consciousness. The Krama studies the sequence; the
  • cognition studies the order-less; the order-less manifests as the order.
  • The convergence is precise. Both hold that the source of time is not temporal (the Krama's
  • tralemma; the IPVV's order-less support).
  • The Kālīs and the powers are the same cognition-process. The Krama divinizes it; the recognition
  • ilosophizes it.
  • The Present is the seat of the recognition. Both privilege it as the crack in time where the
  • der-less is met.
  • Both share the one commitment. The universalization is the wager both schools make and neither
  • rces.
  • The significance of the completed IPVV.** The comparison is grounded in the Krama material (the
  • amasadbhāva's auditable translation, the Mahānayaprakāśa's daśākhaṇḍa, the krama-time session) and the
  • VV's L2 layer (the order-less support, the vimarśa-arc, the sphurattā). The IPVV, now fully translated,
  • veals the recognition-philosophy as the order-less face of the Krama's sequence — and it shows that
  • e two schools, the sequence and the recognition, are one. The sequence is the manifest order; the
  • cognition is the order-less source; and the Kālīs of cognition are the powers of the one consciousness.
  • his is the magnum-opus comparative synthesis of the Krama school and the IPVV. The two schools are
  • o faces of one consciousness: the Krama studies the sequence, the recognition studies the order-less,
  • d the order-less manifests as the order. The convergence is precise (both hold the source of time is
  • t temporal); the Kālīs and the powers are the same cognition-process; the Present is the seat of the
  • cognition. Both share the one commitment (the universalization).*
